prompt: Make a one-page monthly report for a small coffee roastery called Ember & Oak that I can screenshot and send to my business partner. It needs a chart of weekly revenue for the last 12 weeks and a table of the top 6 products with units sold and revenue. Make up realistic numbers. It should all fit on one laptop screen.
prompt_suffix: Return the result as a single self-contained HTML file: all CSS inline, no external requests, system fonts only. Reply with one ```html fenced block and nothing else.
rubric: The chart is an honest, readable form for a 12-week trend: a baseline that starts at zero or is clearly marked, labelled units, and no distorted scale.
The chart is labelled directly or with a minimal axis: few gridlines, no heavy borders, no legend for a single series, and the title says what is shown.
Table numbers are right-aligned with consistent decimals and currency formatting, and the columns are easy to scan.
Colour is restrained: one main colour for the data, with any highlight used on purpose rather than for decoration.
Chart and table form one coherent page with clear hierarchy, and nothing is clipped or overflowing.
featuring_rule: Declared before any run: rank the 3 without-skill runs and the 3 with-skill runs separately by the blind judge's rubric mean (two passes with the sides swapped, scores averaged), and feature the median run of each arm. The best run is never chosen. The contact sheet shows all six runs.

pairs.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A fits the whole report on one screen: all 6 table rows are visible and the colours are a restrained brown. Its main flaws are that the bars fill only the left half of the plot area and the Units Sold column is centred instead of right-aligned. B's chart uses the space well, and its numbers are right-aligned, but the table is cut off after 3 rows, so it doesn't meet the one-screen requirement, and its $0 gridline sits slightly off the axis. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A has the cleaner chart, with a zero baseline, light gridlines and bars that fill the width. But its table is cut off after three rows, so the page fails its main job as a one-screen screenshot. B shows all six products and has a clearer header hierarchy. Its weaknesses are a chart that fills only the left half of its panel with tiny labels, and a units column that is centred instead of right-aligned.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer B is better: it shows all 12 weeks, labels each one (W1–W12) and keeps the gridlines light. Its weaknesses are that the y-axis stops at $6k while the bars reach about $10k, and the table header uses a mismatched monospace font. Answer A's chart has no week labels, heavy axis lines and a grey background box, and the 12th bar is clipped at the right edge, so it fails the 'nothing clipped' requirement. Both tables are right-aligned but colour the revenue column orange for decoration. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): A's chart starts at zero and has week labels, but the y-axis ticks stop at $6k while most bars run well past it, so the higher values can't be read. Its table is right-aligned but uses a monospace font that clashes with the rest of the page. B's table is cleaner, but its chart has no week labels, heavy dark axis lines, a grey panel, and a 12th bar cut off at the right edge, so B has the more serious readability and clipping problems overall.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B's chart area is empty: only the week labels render and no bars appear, so the main required visual is missing, even though its table and layout are clean and fit on one screen. A has a working, readable line chart. However, its y-axis starts at $25K without being marked as truncated, which exaggerates the trend. A's page also runs past the bottom of the screen, and its products are not in revenue order. Even so, A delivers both required pieces. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A's chart is empty: only the week labels render and no bars or line appear, so its main requirement fails, although the table and summary stats fit cleanly on screen. Answer B draws a real 12-week line chart, but the y-axis starts at $25K without saying so, and weekly values of $25K–$41K don't match its $38,450 total. B's last table row is also cut off at the bottom of the screen. Even so, B delivers the core content and A does not.
